entities.summary: Sírna Sáeglach, son of Dian mac Demal, son of Demal mac Rothechtaid, son of Rothechtaid mac Main, was, according to medieval Irish legend and historical tradition, a High King of Ireland. He separated the province of Ulster from the authority of the High King, and is said to have made war against the Ulaid, who had killed his great grandfather, for a hundred years according to the Lebor Gabála Érenn, 150 years according to the Annals of the Four Masters, but Geoffrey Keating, citing an ancient poem, gives him only twenty-one years.

entities.name: Sírna Sáeglach
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sírna Sáeglach ('Sírna the Long-Lived') was, according to medieval Irish legend and historical tradition, the 34th High King of Ireland. His epithet 'Sáeglach' — meaning Long-Lived or of Long Life — suggests either a legendary exceptionally long reign or a mythological tradition of a king whose vitality embodied the land's abundance. He is the grandfather of Gíallchad, the 37th High King, connecting his lineage into the broader legendary king sequence.

Sírna belongs to the deep mythological stratum of the Irish High King lists compiled by monastic scholars in the 8th–10th centuries CE. His long-lived epithet places him in a category of legendary rulers associated with prosperity and supernatural duration — analogous to the antediluvian patriarchs of Genesis (Methuselah, Noah) or the ancient Sumerian kings whose legendary reigns extended for thousands of years. These longevity traditions in Irish, biblical, and Mesopotamian king-lists reflect common ancient Near Eastern narrative patterns about the sacred time of origins.

The Annals of the Four Masters and the Lebor Gabála Érenn preserve Sírna's name as part of the continuous sequence that medieval Irish dynastic culture required to authenticate royal lineage. Dynasties claiming descent from the legendary High Kings cited this unbroken chain as the basis of their rule. In this sense, Sírna Sáeglach's primary historical significance is as a genealogical anchor — a named figure in a deliberate construction of ancient Irish royal memory.
